summary.value: The authors propose a new algorithm SUPO aimed to optimize Llm training in long-horizon multi-turn tasks. Token sequences of increasing length pose a challenge to existing RL pipelines given the significant computational effort in terms of rollouts and memory requirements. In SUPO,  a task-relevant summary of past interactions is identified according to a threshold rule. A policy gradient is estimated based upon token sequences alongside summarization calls. The goal is to jointly optimize multi-turn interactions and summarization strategies. The authors report the results of an empirical testbed on CodeGym (Du et al., 2025) and BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025) wherein SUPO is shown to lead to improved success rates with similar or smaller working context length.

strengths.value:
1. The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem in training LLMs for long horizon multi-turn tasks.

2. The empirical testbed suggests context summarization is an effective way to reduce computational burden.

weaknesses.value: 1. I could not understand the way the context summarization tool is trained. At times the text seems to indicate that the only relevant hyper-parameter is the threshold L. However, this hyper-parameter is only used to determine when a sequence of tokens is considered too long. I fail to see anywhere in the text a clear indication on how the actual summary (which is also a sequence of tokens) is produced.

questions.value:
1. Please describe in detail how a summary sequence of tokens is produced. 

2. There is a literature on how to aggregate states for reinforcement learning.  See for example, the paper by  Singh, Jaakkola and Jordan. In a sense, summarization can be seen as state aggregation. I would like the authors to expand upon the connection of the present work to this literature.

https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/1994/file/287e03db1d99e0ec2edb90d079e142f3-Paper.pdf

comment.value:
Thanks for your time reviewing our paper, we would address your questions in the following. 

---

**W1 & Q1: It is not clearly stated how the actual summary is produced.**

**A:** The mechanism by which the summarization is produced is introduced in Section 2.2, with illustration in Figure 1. Specifically, as you understood, when the context length $|s_t|$ reaches the threshold $L$, the MDP would transit to the next state $s_{t+1}$ ending with a summarization prompt $v_{\mathtt{sum}}$. The LLM is then prompted to generate an action $a_{t+1}$ which (i) is a sequence of tokens, and (ii) contains its summarization of the current working context. That is how the summarization is generated. 

---

**Q2: Connection with the literature on state aggregation for RL:**

**A:** Thank for bringing up this pioneer work! Our method is definitely related in spirit to this classical work on state aggregation by [SJJ], who propose mapping a large Markov decision process into a smaller “cluster space” via probabilistic assignments $P(x | s)$. There are both similarities and strict differences between summarization-augmented MDP we consider and the soft state aggregation method in [SJJ]. 

- Summarization corresponds to compressing the rich interaction history into a more compact representation used for control. Just as soft state aggregation replaces the original state with a lower-dimensional cluster representation for learning, our framework replaces the ever-growing raw trajectory with learned summaries that feed back into the agent’s decision process.
- However, the key difference is that: In soft state aggregation [SJJ], the compression is done by a **fixed mapping**, optionally updated slowly by a separate heuristic like ASA. The RL algorithm itself treats this mapping as exogenous. In our framework, the “aggregator” is the policy $\pi_{\theta}$ (which is the LLM here) itself that produces *natural-language summaries* conditioned on the full interaction history and task context. By such a modeling strategy, we can jointly train the policy to make decisions for the original task as well as generate summarization (or state aggregation) via an end-to-end RL objective. This makes summarization or state aggregator a *policy component* rather than a fixed feature map.

We have added the above discussion to the related work section in the revised version.

---

Again, we would like to thank you for your valuable time reviewing our paper. We hope our response can address your questions regarding how the summary is generated and how our work connect to the soft state aggregation method. However, we are still unable to figure out the reason that our work is receiving a rating of 2 (reject) based on your questions. We are more than happy to address any further concerns or questions on our paper. In the meanwhile, we would appreciate it if you find our paper worth a higher score. Thank you!

comment.value:
I remain unclear about the “summarization-augmented MDP” concept: 

• Summaries are stochastic functions of the entire history, not the current state. Hence the process is not Markovian: the “summary” is itself a learned compression of history, not fully determined by the state.
• The “reset to initial prompt + summary” rule is not a standard MDP transition. It is a non-local state transformation depending on history length.

The paper does not provide clear definitions on:
• action space for summarization
• constrains that define a valid summary is,
•reward function to evaluate quality of summaries.

summary.value: This paper addresses the critical challenge of context length limitations in reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning for long-horizon multi-turn tool use with large language models (LLMs). The proposed SUmmarization augmented Policy Optimization (SUPO) algorithm formulates this as an end-to-end RL problem, optimizing both tool-use behaviors and summarization strategies.

strengths.value:
- SUPO is the RL-based approach to seamlessly integrate summarization as a core component of the training process, effectively breaking the context length barrier. 

- The algorithm demonstrates robust performance gains on both coding (CodeGym) and web search (BrowseComp-Plus) benchmarks.

weaknesses.value:
- The novelty of the paper is relatively weak. The innovation point of summarization-augmented is essentially no different from agent memory [1] [2].

- The reinforcement learning idea of SUPO is also widely applied. There are many works combining reinforcement learning and agent memory [3]. The authors did not conduct comparisons in the experimental section. Comparing only with GRPO is limited.

- The related work also mentions Memory-r1. It designs adding, updating, or deleting entries in an external memory base. I do not think, as the authors claim, that it lacks the capability for summarization and compression. Choosing appropriate add, update, and delete operations is precisely summarization and compression.  Moreover, adding summarization and compression is just a matter of prompting and does not constitute a significant improvement.


[1] Zhang, Zeyu, et al. "A survey on the memory mechanism of large language model-based agents." ACM Transactions on Information Systems 43.6 (2025): 1-47.

[2] Wang, Zora Zhiruo, et al. "Agent workflow memory." arXiv preprint arXiv:2409.07429 (2024).

[3] Yan, Sikuan, et al. "Memory-r1: Enhancing large language model agents to manage and utilize memories via reinforcement learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.19828 (2025).

- Why in Equation (1) is it $v_{sum} \subseteq s_t$? Shouldn't it be $v_{sum} \supseteq s_t$?

- Why in the related work does it say that compared to MemAgent, “Our framework further subsumes more general multi-turn tool using problems”? What advantages does SUPO have over MemAgent?

- Can the authors compare with Memory-R1 empirically? Because the SUPO combining reinforcement learning and agent memory, but does not compare with related work, which weakens the credibility of the paper's contributions.

comment.value:
Thank you for your insightful feedbacks for improving the quality of our paper! We would address all your concerns and questions in the sequel. 

---

**W1: The novelty of the paper is relatively weak, and the innovation is no different from [1][2].**

**A:** We could not agree that our innovation is no different from existing agent memory works [1][2]. We explain the key differences and highlight our novelty in the following:

1. Firstly, our scope is different from most existing works: we aim to use the summarization-based context management mechanism to scale the RL training performance of multi-turn tool use LLM agents, which is not present in the works in the survey [1]. Also, compared to the specific work of [2], they aim to share the problem solving routine across different problem instances, which is different from our focus — using memory to augment the agent to handle a single long-horizon problem instance.
2. Secondly, most of the prior works in [1] as well as the work of [2] do not consider using RL for training memory augmented agents. Our work propose to use agent memory to scale multi-turn tool-use RL training beyond the working context limits. We highlight that our scope is also different from the other recent papers on RL for agent memory, including Memory-R1 and MemAgent you mentioned, since their focus is on long-context QA problem. We explain in more detail the difference with Memory-R1 and MemAgent in the responses to your following questions.
3. Finally, we emphasize that in order to realize our idea of scaling multi-turn RL training with summarization-based context management, we bring several innovations in terms of problem formulation and algorithm design. Specifically, we propose a rigorous MDP formulation and a new algorithm SUPO. SUPO requires multi-trajectory rollout handling with (i) shared rollout-level advantages calculation and (ii) overlong masking. We also implemented a strict working-context control mechanism to ensure the trajectory length behaves properly during RL training. All these components actually require careful code level design and optimization for efficiency and performance.

---

**W2, W3 & Q4: Comparison with RL method Memory-R1 [3].**

**A:** Thanks for bringing the nice work of [3] up! However, we need to point out that despite both SUPO and Memory-R1 utilize RL method for agent memory, the scope of the two works are actually quite different and thus are not directly comparable. We provide a more in-depth comparison of our work with Memory-R1 in the following: 

1. Firstly and most importantly, Memory-R1 focuses on the task of QA based on multi-session dialogue, where RL is applied to memory managing agent and question answering agent separately. For the memory agent, the protocol between each time of memory update is a single-turn process, i.e., reading the current dialogue chunk. In contrast, we focus on multi-turn tool use tasks, e.g., deep research. Our agent needs to handle multiple rounds of tool-using between each time of memory updates, and the summarization capability is jointly trained with the tool use behavior in an end-to-end manner. Thus, we are answering a different question than Memory-R1, that is, can we utilize summarization-based context management to scale RL training for long-horizon multi-turn tool use tasks like deep research? Memory-R1 is not designed for such problems and is unknown how to apply. From such a perspective, SUPO and Memory-R1 just formulate and solve different problems and are not directly comparable.
2. Secondly, the utility of memory is also different. In our case, the summarization serves as a tool to enable efficient and stable training of a *single* long-horizon task. E.g., completing a single deep research query of a user. In contrast, the memory in Memory-R1 is to improve the QA capability of downstream agents across multiple past dialogue sessions. This also makes the scope of two works different. 
3. Thirdly, we would appreciate the reviewer’s comments on our comparison with Memory-R1. We have revised the paper to make the description more accurate. However, we do not agree with the reviewer’s comment that “adding summarization and compression is just a matter of prompting and does not constitute a significant improvement”. In long-horizon tasks we consider, the trajectory could grow up to 64K before each time of summarization, and the quality of summarization and compression of useful information in the current trajectory is key to enable stable training of such multi-turn tool use agents. We observe stable improvement of the summarization quality of the agent we train from different perspectives. Firstly, we observe improved conditional successful rates given rollouts with summarization, see Section 4.2.1. Secondly, we provide case studies for the quality of summarization of the agent before and after SUPO in Appendix D.1. The improved summarization quality essentially leads to the success after training.

comment.value:
**Q1: In Fig 1, do the last three lines all start with s1?**

**A:** Nice observation! Yes as you see all the last three lines start with $s_1$. In our notation $s_1$ refers to the original question and system prompts, and our agent state evolution keeps the original question and the prompts in the beginning after each time of summarization, that’s why each state $s_t$ has prefix $s_1$. We have made this clearer by adding explanations in the caption of Figure 1.

---

**Q2: Notations in Equation (1).**

**A:** According to our notation (in the beginning of Section 2), for any two token sequences $s_0$ and $s_1$, we say $s_0\subseteq s_1$ if $s_0$ is a subsequence of $s_1$. Thus when the summarization prompt $v_{\mathtt{sum}}$ is appended to the previous state, we can verify that now $v_{\mathtt{sum}}\subseteq s_t$.

---

**Q3: What advantages does SUPO have over MemAgent?**

**A:** Thanks for the clarification question! We again highlight that our framework as well as the experiments consider a strictly larger class of problems than most of the recent agent-memory-training works, including MemAgent. Specifically, compared with MemAgent paper:

- The MemAgent paper considers the problem of long context QA, where the agent passively read chunks one by one and update the memory. In contrast, our paper focuses on training multi-turn tool use LLM agents, where the agent need to sophisticatedly and actively use the tools for multiple turns, and properly summarize the trajectories *generated by itself*.
- Long context QA can be viewed as a special case of our framework with (i) only single turn between summarization, where in SUPO there are multiple-turns between summarization; (ii) no additional tool use, since the agent only needs to summarize the new chunks and update the memory, where in our paper the agent needs to use different tools for multiple turns.
- In our work, we train the agent to simultaneously master (i) using the problem-specific tools and (ii) correctly update the summary of history to jointly optimize the problem solving performance in an end-to-end manner. In contrast, the work of MemAgent does not consider how to perform end-to-end training of such a multi-turn tool use agent with summarization.

---

Overall, we really appreciate the insightful questions and suggestions the reviewer proposed. We have revised our paper accordingly. Meanwhile, we have highlighted the contributions of our paper (as well as in the global comments) in comparison with other works on Memory and RL, and why it is not directly comparable. We are happy to take any further questions and discussion. We would appreciate it if you find our paper worth a higher score. Thank you!

summary.value:
The paper studies the use of RL on LLMs that use summarization-based context management. That is, given that periodic LLM-generated summaries are produced before resetting the working context to the initial prompt, how can we train the LLM to handle this structure most effectively? 

This is formalized as a summarization-augmented MDP with a transition rule that triggers summarization once a threshold L is exceeded, then starts the following segment from the prompt \+ the summary. The authors derive a policy-gradient representation that decomposes the long rollout into a sum of gradients over summarized sub-trajectories, enabling drop-in use of standard policy-gradient methods. 

They instantiate the framework as SUPO and evaluate on CodeGym and BrowseComp-Plus. SUPO improves success rates relative to GRPO without summarization under the same or smaller working context, as well as ablations, and it scales at test time as the number of summary rounds increases beyond those used during training.

strengths.value:
* **Precise problem framing & principled setup.** The summarization-augmented MDP cleanly captures context resets and explicitly shows how summaries enter the dynamics.  
* **Practical algorithmic choices.** Overlong masking and the group-relative advantage are well-motivated and ablated.  
* **Compelling empirical results.** Across two distinct multi-turn tasks, SUPO achieves higher accuracy with narrower working windows than GRPO, and promising test-time scaling.

weaknesses.value:
* **Theory positioning.** Theorem 2.2 appears to be a particular case of the standard policy-gradient theorem (partitioning the sum at summary indices), since the setting is still an MDP. The paper could be clearer that this is an immediate corollary rather than a fundamentally new theorem. Additionally, if this is the case, much of the theoretical discussion would benefit from being trimmed down for leanness.  
* **Minor clarity/typos.** There are multiple scattered grammar issues that should be polished before camera-ready.

Overall, the contribution seems limited, as the paper essentially uses a slight variant of GRPO to train the LLM in this summarization setting, without any significant conceptual or methodological contribution. I am open to changing my assessment of this based on the discussion with the authors.

questions.value:
1. In what precise sense does Thm. 2.2 go beyond the classic policy-gradient theorem? From the derivation, it seems to be a partition of the standard sum. Could you clarify whether any usual assumption (e.g., Markovian dynamics, stationarity) fails and thus requires this adaptation?  
2. **Figure 5 variant definitions.** For each figure, please specify the max number of summaries/tokens (S).   
3. Beyond the positive scaling in Figure 5, do you observe a point where additional summaries hurt due to information loss or drift? Could you provide any analysis of summary content quality (e.g., factual retention rate) as (S) grows?

comment.value:
Thank you for your insightful feedbacks for improving the quality of our paper! We would address all your concerns and questions in the sequel. 

---

**W1 & Q1:  How does Theorem 2.2 go beyond classic PG? Is there any adaption different from usual assumptions? If not, relevant discussions can be trimmed down for leanness.**  

**A:** We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestions and we clarify Theorem 2.2 and corresponding theoretical discussions as follows: 

1. The theorem is based on the same derivation as the standard policy-gradient result, but is organized in a way that best explains the validity of our proposed algorithm SUPO. In that sense, it is more like a corollary of the standard PG and only relies on usual assumptions like Markovian and stationarity. We have made this point clearer in the revision.
2. However, we still need the discussion to clearly convey the idea behind SUPO and its theoretical validity. Specifically, for agents with summarization-based (or even more complicated) context management, the state evolution is no longer the same as the vanilla ReAct agent that always simply concats the next token to the working context. For ReAct agent, such simplicity allows one to obtain the policy gradient of each generated token (action) efficiently by directly working on the single final trajectory (thus a single forward pass of the LLM can calculate the probability for each token in the trajectory). However, for agent with context management, the rollout involves more complicated state transitions which are not simple concatenations of next tokens all the time, e.g., deletion of the history. This may in turn complicate the calculation of PG since we can not handle the gradient of each token by simply viewing the rollout as a single long trajectory as in ReAct. 
3. Now what we want to show by Theorem 2.2 is that for the summarization-based context management we study, the policy gradient can still be efficiently calculated by viewing the rollout as $I+1$ separate trajectories, where $I$ is the number of summarization. Such a perspective provides the validity of SUPO we implemented in the experiments.

---

**W2: The contribution is limited due to lack of significant conceptual or methodological contributions.** 

**A:** We point out that the contribution of the paper is *not* simply a *sligh*t variant of GRPO. Let’s explain our contributions in more detail to address your concerns: 

1. The MDP formulation to tackle the long-context problem in multi-turn tool use RL is new and necessary. Prior RL agent papers using GRPO (e.g., Search-R1, ToolRL) cannot train beyond the context limit due to the naive context management approach. However, the context length limit quickly becomes key bottleneck to scale the application of LLM agents to more and more complex tasks. Our paper lays out a conception foundation for future works to explore other methods for training the agent to actively manage its working context during both training and test-time inference.
2. At the algorithmic level, SUPO is also not a minor modification of vanilla GRPO. SUPO requires multi-trajectory rollout handling with (i) shared rollout-level advantages calculation and (ii) overlong masking. We also implemented a strict working-context control mechanism to ensure the trajectory length behaves properly during RL training. All these components actually require careful code level design and optimization for efficiency and performance. Empirically, we achieved stable training of the agent beyond the fixed context length for the multi-turn tool use tasks including deep research, which is not achieved by existing prior works with GRPO training. Extensive ablations have also confirmed the importance of the algorithmic components we involve, providing insights for future research in this direction. 
3. Finally, we refer to our answers to **Reviewer t1mf W1** for further clarification of the contribution and novelty of our paper in the line of works on agent memory.

---

**W3: Multiple scattered grammar issues:**

**A:** Thank you for your careful review of our manuscript, and we have polished the writing to minimize the grammar issues in the revision.

comment.value:
**Q2: What is the maximum number of summaries/tokens in Figure 5?** 

**A:** We clarify Figure 5 as following: As mentioned in Section 4.3, we experimented with 5 different choices of maximum round of summary $S\in\{1, 2, 5, 11, 23\}$, and for each $S$, the effective maximum number of tokens are $65536 \times (S+1)$ as we defined in Section 4.1 (Implementations and baselines). Each curve in Figure 5 involves 5 points which are accuracies corresponding to running the trained agent with $S\in\{1, 2, 5, 11, 23\}$.

---

**Q3: Could additional summaries hurt due to information loss? Can we analyze summary quality as S grows?** 

**A:** This is a good question! We answer your question from the following two perspectives:

- From the perspective of final accuracy on the evaluation set, there is not hurt for involving larger maximum round of summarization. The reason is that giving more rounds of summarization, e.g., from $S=5$ to $S=11$, the agent could only get more questions right: The questions that have already been solved within $5$ rounds of summarization would also be solved within $5$ rounds even we set $S=11$ in our deterministic evaluation. For those that fail to be solved within $5$ rounds, either the agent produced a wrong answer before hitting the budget, or the agent just runs out of summarization round. So increasing $S$ would then benefit completing questions of the second type of failure under smaller $S$. That’s why the curves in Figure 5 are all monotonic.
- Regarding the summarization quality as $S$ increases, it is not trivial to design rigorous experiments to test it, because the quality of each new round of summarization depends on both the summarization of last round and the new trajectory generated in this round. Intuitively, the quality of summarization itself should not decrease as $S$ increases since all the summarizations are generated conditioning on a context shorter than $L$. It could be the case that some information is lost after multiple rounds of summary. But as long as the most useful facts to complete the task are retained, the summarization should be considered as good. And such a capability to keep the most useful information is trained in an end-to-end manner via SUPO. We provide additional case studies in the revised paper to showcase the improvement of the summarization quality after SUPO in Appendix D.1.

---

Overall, we really appreciate the insightful questions and suggestions the reviewer proposed. We have revised our paper accordingly. Meanwhile, we have highlighted the contributions of the paper in our responses. We are happy to take any further questions and discussions, and we would appreciate it if you find our paper worth a higher score. Thank you!
